newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BAe brags of recovery as profits soar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BAe brags of recovery as profits soar.

text.p: British Aerospace announced a sharp jump in profits on Wednesday and boasted of its recovery from a disastrous diversification into cars and property.

Pretax profits leapt by over 80 percent to 425 million pounds ($696 million) last year, from 234 million in 1995, on sales up 12.2 percent to 7.44 billion pounds. The final dividend was increased to 9.375 pence from 7.5p making 15.625 pence for the year on earnings of 67.1 pence.

Underlying profits before exceptional charges rose 38 percent to 456 million pounds from 330 million last time, underpinned by a jump in operating profits from defence rising to 553 million pounds from 487 million in 1995.
The company said the result was driven by record orders and strong margins after radical restructuring in recent years returned the group's focus to its core businesses of aerospace and defence.
"It is very easy to forget we were 1.2 billion pounds in debt four years ago," finance director Richard Lapthorne told Reuters in an interview.
"In 1996 there was a 52 percent increase in earnings per share off higher sales at better margins producing a really exceptional (net) cash position of 726 million at the year end," he said.

The company said a 1.9 billion pound British order for Nimrod maritime patrol aircraft helped boost its order book to an all-time high of 19.4 billion pounds by the end of the year, compared to 17.1 billion a year ago.
Chief executive Sir Richard Evans said a further 1.2 billion pounds of defence orders from Britain, Australia and Qatar have been booked in since the end of the year.

With a strong order book tucked under its arm, Evans said senior management could now concentrate on the consolidation of the European aerospace industry to match the might of U.S. rivals led by Boeing and Lockheed Martin.
Evans told Reuters the priority for the European effort was the current move to get the four-nation Airbus Industrie consortium restructured as a single company.
He played down speculation that BAe was looking at a full merger with Britain's General Electric Co Plc.
"We have always maintained despite all the speculation that goes on about strategic moves and all the rest of it that Airbus is the driver for what is going to happen in Europe," he told Reuters.

"Nothing is in and nothing is out. The GEC position is a part of the European position and obviously in the context of Europe and the whole European scene we talk to GEC in the same way as we talk to all of the other players. But the driver for us is the consequence of restructuring Airbus," he said.

The company declines to detail profits from its work making wings for Airbus, in which it holds a 20 percent stake. But BAe's Commercial Aerospace division which includes the Airbus business cut operating losses last year to 78 million pounds from 118 million in 1995.
According to industry sources losses from its troubled regional aircraft businesses were likely to have been over 100 million pounds last year.

But the company says it has got the situation under control, with its Avro regional jets business on target to break even this year and production at the Jetstream turboprop business now cut to 10 aircraft a year from 20 previously, against an orderbook for 12 aircraft.
"Clearly with an order book in excess of one year (of work) we have a fair number of options still," finance director Richard Lapthorne said.
